entries.title: The DOJ Is Investigating Networks that Halted White House Pool Coverage
entries.summary: The TV pool of five broadcasters last month ceased presidential coverage after the administration barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
entries.content:
By Alanna Durkin Richer and Amy Taxin

The Department of Justice is investigating whether the decision of the White House television press pool to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month violated antitrust law, an agency spokesperson said Saturday.

Emily Covington, a spokesperson for the department, said group boycotts among business competitors might violate U.S. law.

“The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” she said.

The announcement came after the television pool of five broadcasters last month ceased presidential coverage after the administration barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.

Messages were sent late Saturday to the five outlets seeking comment: ABC, CBS, CNN, FOX and NBC.

The White House press pool, which is a rotating cast of news outlets that covers the president, has become a proxy for the wider fight over whether the president, or anyone, can control the content of news reports — a type of free speech, pillar of American democracy.

Last month's developments marked an extraordinary escalation in Trump’s efforts to restrict news reporters and outlets that he finds insufficiently supportive.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued over the days-long ban. It was lifted after a judge handed the three news organizations a reprieve, which is in place until Tuesday.

Television pool coverage of the White House has also resumed.

Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists' regional director of the Americas, on Saturday criticized the administration's decision to investigate.

“The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access,” Zamora said on X. “The public’s right to know depends on that access.”
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Six Senators Call for Trump to Reverse Course on Russia Diesel Purchase
entries.summary: The four Republicans and two Democrats say the U.S. shouldn't give Putin a financial lifeline.
entries.content:
By Kevin Freking

A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.

Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.

Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute.

“The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote.

The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.

Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan.

“We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said.

Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine.

The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war.

“Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law."

Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law.

“The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS's “Face the Nation.”

He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month.

“This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said.

Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Trump Declares That Russia and Ukraine Have Agreed to an ‘Energy Ceasefire’
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he did not know about the agreement on the energy ceasefire before Trump’s social media post.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an “energy ceasefire,” a truce that could significantly impact the ongoing conflict as attacks on energy infrastructure remain a central component of both countries’ war efforts.

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote Sunday on Truth Social.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Axios that Trump’s energy ceasefire announcement “was news for me.”

“But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree,” Zelenskyy added.

The White House referred The Washington Sun to the president’s Truth Social post when asked for a comment.

Since the start of the four-year-long war, Russia has been targeting Ukraine’s heating and electricity facilities while Ukraine has launched attacks on Russia’s oil refineries.

Trump has criticized Zelenskyy for the impact of Ukraine’s strikes on Russia’s diesel fuel refineries, a move that has further exacerbated the global fuel supply already constrained by the U.S. war with Iran.

“We told him, do whatever you want, but don't hit the diesel fuel because there's a big problem, big shortage. And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel,” Trump told reporters on Friday.

“He better damn well stop!” Trump added.

Several Republicans have called for an end to the war with the midterms approaching and rising fuel prices putting pressure on the U.S. farming industry.

Zelenskyy, in an interview with ABC’s “This Week,” hit back against Trump and others who have blamed him for the continuing war with Russia and the impact on the global energy supply.

“Because it's more difficult to stop Putin than to pressure others. Because it's more simple to speak about the prices and connect it with Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said Sunday. “When everybody in the world understands because of the war in the Middle East, the prices are rising.”

Trump announced on Friday that the U.S. had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to “immediately” send hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the American marketplace.

The president said that between the Russian diesel deal and the U.S.’s “TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz” — a key waterway for the flow of the global oil supply located in the Middle East — that diesel prices for American consumers will be “COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!”

“Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel,” Trump wrote Friday on Truth Social.

The initial shipment of 300,000 tons, which would be about 2.25 million barrels of oil, would equal less than a day of U.S. oil usage, with America consuming approximately 20.6 million barrels of petroleum per day according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Striking a deal with Russia for their oil appears to be a departure from Trump’s previous position on the issue. In September 2025, Trump called on NATO countries to stop buying Russian oil and put 50% to 100% tariffs on China for its purchases of the Russian energy source.

“It greatly weakens your negotiating position, and bargaining power, over Russia,” Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time, in a post addressed to the NATO nations.

Congress also just passed a new law, named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would sanction the biggest countries buying oil from Russia.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Trump Administration Plans $65 Million Exhibit at Saudi Arabia’s ‘Expo 2030’
entries.summary: Out: Climate and diversity. In: America’s friendship with Saudi Arabia.
entries.content:
The State Department is laying the groundwork for its exhibit at Expo 2030, the latest in a series of global gatherings that occur every five years. Host nation Saudi Arabia expects 197 nations to participate in the six-month-long world’s fair-style event.

The United States’ exhibit in Riyadh is expected to cost between $55 and $65 million and will deliver a “multisensory celebration of American excellence,” per previously unreported documents obtained by The Washington Sun.

“U.S. pavilions at World Expos are public and commercial diplomacy platforms for engaging foreign audiences, promoting American values and prosperity, advancing U.S. bilateral and regional goals, and showcasing American culture and technology,” reads a request for information document recently posted to a federal contracting website.

The event, the document says, “offers the United States Government an opportunity to inform and inspire foreign audiences about the United States, its people, values, and foreign policies, and to promote U.S. economic and commercial interests.”

The request for information document is broadly similar to the one sent out ahead of Expo 2025, which took place in Osaka, Japan.

But the Trump administration put its mark on the plans. A reference to the multinational Kigali Amendment aimed at curbing emissions does not appear in the Expo 2030 plan as it had in the 2025 document.

Nor does a line stating that the “USA Pavilion is nonpolitical and nonpartisan in nature, of the highest possible quality, and balanced and representative of the diversity of American political, social, and cultural life.”

Added to the Expo 2030 document is the listed objective that the exhibit “demonstrate America’s value as a champion of, and trusted partner in, preserving cultural heritage and ecology.”

“Particular emphasis will be placed on our bilateral relationship with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” the document says. “This goal centers regional audiences, establishing the American legacy of constructive engagement and partnership in the region.”

The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
entries.author: Mark Alfred
